text.title: Freelancer Rate Raise Letter Template Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every retainer rate-raise letter MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The new rate's effective date MUST be at least 30 calendar days after the letter date, at least one full billing cycle for a monthly retainer, and no shorter than the notice period the retainer contract names for rate changes, whichever is longest. "Effective immediately" and "from your next invoice" are rejected. A single client MUST NOT receive more than one rate change in any 12-month window unless the scope changed materially and the change is documented.

rationale.source: Retainer-contract notice-clause practice; widely established freelance pricing guidance

rule.rationale: A raise with no runway reads as an ultimatum and gives the client a budget problem instead of a decision. Thirty days is the minimum most finance teams need to re-approve a line item; a full cycle means the client never sees the old and new rate on the same invoice. Two raises in a year signals the first one was mispriced and invites a renegotiation of both.

rule.statement: The letter MUST cite at least one measurable value delta delivered inside this engagement since the current rate was set (a named deliverable, a metric moved, scope or responsibility added, a capability the client now depends on), quoted from the source of record named in `inputs_used`. Inflation, CPI, "market rates" or "my costs have gone up" MAY appear only as a secondary sentence and MUST NOT be the sole justification.

rationale.source: Value-based pricing practice; methodology design (AGENTS.md: price justified by value delta, not CPI)

rule.rationale: A CPI justification tells the client the freelancer is a cost line that tracks inflation, which is exactly the framing procurement uses to cap it. A value delta tells them what they would lose. "Since March I own the release pipeline you previously paid an agency for" survives a budget review; "costs have risen 6%" does not.

rule.statement: The letter MUST state exactly one new rate as a number with currency and unit (per hour, per day, per month retainer), the current rate in the same unit, and the percentage change. Ranges, "starting from", "we can discuss the exact figure" and any wording that leaves the number open are rejected.

rationale.source: Anchoring effect (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974); negotiation practice

rule.rationale: The first number stated becomes the reference point for everything that follows. A range invites the client to anchor on its bottom; an open figure invites them to propose one. One number, with the old rate beside it so the increase is visibly reasonable, is the only shape that lets the client say yes without a meeting.

rule.statement: The letter MUST list every signed statement of work, accepted quote or prepaid retainer period in flight and state that each completes at the current rate. The new rate applies only to work agreed after the effective date. Repricing agreed work is forbidden.

rationale.source: Contract practice: agreed terms bind until varied by both parties

rule.rationale: Applying a new rate to a signed SOW is a unilateral contract change, and the client's finance team will treat it as one. Naming the in-flight items and protecting them costs nothing and converts the letter from "prices went up" into "here is exactly what changes and what does not", which is what makes a busy client approve it without escalation.

rule.statement: The letter MUST NOT contain a discount, an alternative lower rate, a "if this is difficult let me know" clause or any fallback. Exactly one pre-decided concession (for example: current rate locked for three further months against an annual prepayment, or a reduced-scope tier) MUST be recorded in the artefact for use only in the T+7 follow-up if the client pushes back.

rationale.source: Widely established negotiation practice: do not concede before the counterparty has responded

rule.rationale: A concession inside the announcement is a negotiation against oneself: the client reads the fallback as the real price and the headline as an opening bid. Holding one prepared concession for the follow-up keeps the letter clean and gives the freelancer a considered answer to push-back instead of an improvised discount.

rule.statement: Before the letter is sent the client MUST be classified stay / negotiate / churn in the artefact, with the evidence for the class: the client's share of the freelancer's trailing-12-month revenue, their realistic alternatives, most recent feedback or NPS, payment behaviour, and any renewal date. If the client exceeds 30% of revenue and is classified churn, the artefact MUST contain a replacement-revenue plan (named pipeline, expected close dates) before the letter goes out.

rationale.source: Client-concentration risk practice (a single client above roughly a quarter to a third of revenue is commonly treated as concentration risk); methodology design (churn-risk classifier ships with the letter)

rule.rationale: The letter is a bet, and the classification is the stake. Raising a client who is 40% of revenue without knowing what happens if they walk is how a freelancer turns a pricing exercise into a cash crisis. The classifier does not stop the raise; it forces the plan for the worst branch to exist before the branch can happen.

rule.statement: A follow-up MUST be scheduled for 7 days after the letter with one concrete path forward per response state: confirmed (send updated retainer terms for signature), no reply (short reminder with the effective date restated), push-back (offer the single prepared concession or a scope call). Silence MUST NOT be treated as acceptance: the new rate is applied only after the client has acknowledged it in writing, and the artefact records the acknowledgement.

rationale.source: Methodology design (post-letter follow-up at T+7); contract-variation practice

rule.rationale: The letter most clients never answer is the one that was read, forwarded to finance and forgotten. Invoicing the new rate on the strength of silence produces a disputed invoice and a relationship conversation the freelancer did not choose. A dated follow-up with a decided next move per outcome turns the raise into a closed loop instead of an open question.

rule.statement: The letter MUST NOT contain apology or hedging language ("sorry", "unfortunately", "I hate to", "I hope this is okay", "I understand if") or a personal-cost narrative (rent, living costs, family). It MUST be under 250 words, open with the value delivered, state the change, state what is protected, and close with the effective date and the follow-up date. Reviewers check against the banned-phrase list.

rationale.source: Methodology design: raise announcement, not a difficult-conversations lecture; business-communication practice

rule.rationale: An apologetic letter asks the client for permission the freelancer does not need and signals the number is negotiable. A personal-cost story invites the client to evaluate the freelancer's finances instead of the value. The business-notice register is the one that gets filed and approved rather than answered and argued.
